title: Roundtree v. City of Page
description: Whether an initiative proposed by residents of the City of Page, which seeks to prevent the narrowing of a specific street, is legislative in nature and therefore falls within the citizens' right to initiate laws at the local level.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the initiative is legislative in nature, creating policy and a permanent rule, and thus falls within citizens' right to initiate laws, or alternatively, that the constitution authorizes initiatives on any matter, not just legislation.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the initiative is administrative, not legislative, as it merely implements existing City policy and supplants administrative authority, and therefore is not a valid subject for a citizen initiative.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' decision and reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that the proposed initiative is legislative in nature and can proceed to the ballot.

title: Smith v. Fontes
description: Whether A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A), which mandates double counting of some invalid signatures for initiative petitions, is unconstitutional as applied because it effectively raises the constitutional 15% signature threshold, thereby hindering the ability of initiatives to qualify for the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs challenged the 'Make Elections Fair Act' initiative's eligibility for the ballot, arguing it failed to meet constitutional signature requirements and that the statute's application should have disqualified it.
defendant_argument: The defendants, specifically Make Elections Fair PAC, argued that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) was unconstitutional as applied because its double counting mechanism effectively raised the 15% signature threshold, and without this unconstitutional application, the Initiative would have qualified.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment dismissing the challenge to the Initiative, ruling that A.R.S. § 19-121.04(A) was unconstitutional as applied because it impermissibly raised the signature threshold, thus allowing the Initiative to qualify for the ballot.

title: Knight v. Fontes
description: Whether the geographic voting districts for court of appeals judges, as defined by A.R.S. § 12-120.02, violate the Free and Equal Elections Clause and the Equal Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Arizona Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The geographic voting districts disenfranchise voters and give unequal weight to votes, arguing that statewide jurisdiction of the court of appeals mandates statewide retention elections.
defendant_argument: The statute is constitutional, as there is no underlying right to vote in every court of appeals judge's retention election, and the one-person, one-vote principle does not apply to the judiciary.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order dismissing the plaintiffs' claim, ruling that the retention election process for court of appeals judges is constitutional.

title: Sync Title Agency, LLC v. Arizona Corporation Commission
description: Whether Sync Title Agency, LLC, is liable for selling unregistered securities and committing securities fraud, with the plaintiff arguing for a non-public offering exemption and against fraud findings, and the defendant arguing against the exemption and for the fraud findings.
plaintiff_argument: Sync argued that the sale of membership interest was an exempt non-public offering, that it had a constitutional right to a jury trial for alleged securities fraud violations, and that the Commission's findings of securities fraud were not supported by substantial evidence.
defendant_argument: The Arizona Corporation Commission argued that Sync sold an unregistered, non-exempt security and committed securities fraud through misrepresentations and omissions, and that Arizona law does not grant a jury-trial right for Commission enforcement actions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, vacating the Commission's order in part, and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its decision. It found Sync participated in the sale, denied a jury trial right, but concluded the offering was exempt from registration. It also found some fraud claims were puffery or had a reasonable basis, but upheld the fraud finding regarding the personal use of investment funds.

title: Francisco v. Affiliated Urologists
description: Whether a warning required by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regarding the use of prescription medication can serve to establish the standard of care and obviate the need for expert testimony in medical malpractice cases.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that FDA black box warnings could establish the standard of care without expert testimony, that their claim was an informed consent case not requiring expert testimony, and that the statutory expert testimony requirements violated the anti-abrogation clause.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that expert medical testimony was required to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice cases, that FDA warnings alone are insufficient, and that the statutory requirements did not violate the anti-abrogation clause.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals' decision and affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that FDA black box warnings cannot substitute for expert testimony to establish the standard of care in medical malpractice cases.

title: Gilpin v. Harris
description: Whether defendants adjudicated 'guilty except insane' (GEI) are criminally responsible for their actions and thus liable for victim restitution.
plaintiff_argument: Lisa Gilpin, as a victim, argued that Marcos Martinez, a GEI defendant, should pay restitution under Arizona's Victims' Bill of Rights, asserting that GEI defendants are criminally responsible.
defendant_argument: Marcos Martinez argued that a GEI judgment is not a 'conviction' for restitution purposes, and therefore restitution was unavailable, relying on the precedent set in State v. Heartfield.
decision_outcome: The court overruled the precedent set in State v. Heartfield and held that restitution is available from defendants adjudged 'guilty except insane' when their actions caused or threatened death or serious injury, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Gilmore v. Gallego
description: Whether the 'release time' provisions in the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the City of Phoenix and the American Federation of Federal, State and Municipal Employees, Local 2384 (the 'Union'), which allow city employees to perform union activities while being paid by the city, violate the Arizona Constitution's Gift Clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, Mark Gilmore and Mark Harder, argued that the release time provisions violate their free-speech, free-association, and right-to-work rights, and the Gift Clause of the Arizona Constitution, contending that if the City pays for it, it constitutes an illegal gift.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Kate Gallego, the City of Phoenix, and the Union, argued that the release time provisions do not violate the employees' free-speech, free-association, or right-to-work rights because the employees do not pay for release time, and do not violate the Gift Clause because they serve a public purpose and are supported by adequate consideration.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' opinion, reversed the trial court's decision, and remanded the case for entry of judgment in favor of the Employees on the Gift Clause claim, finding the release time provisions unconstitutional.

title: Pima County. v. State
description: Whether the State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses that exceed the Arizona Constitution's 1% Limit on residential property taxes as "additional state aid for education" following the 2018 legislative amendments to A.R.S. § 15-910, and whether these taxes continue to be "primary property taxes" eligible for reimbursement.
plaintiff_argument: The State must reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses because the 2018 amendments to § 15-910 are unworkable, do not trump constitutional limitations, and do not eliminate the State's reimbursement obligation for primary property taxes.
defendant_argument: The State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County because the 2018 amendments reclassified desegregation expenses as a new type of secondary property tax, which is not eligible for state reimbursement under § 15-972(E), and these amendments are constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State is not obligated to reimburse Pima County for desegregation expenses, affirming the court of appeals' opinion.

title: Mitchell v. Palmer
description: Whether the Maricopa County Attorney's Office (MCAO) should be disqualified from prosecuting Tamira Durand's case because one of its employees is a victim in the case, with the State arguing against disqualification and Durand arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the victim-employee's conflict was not imputed to the entire office, there was no appearance of impropriety, and their screening procedure was adequate to avoid conflict, thus disqualification was unwarranted.
defendant_argument: Durand argued that her due process rights would be violated if prosecuted by an agency with a conflict of interest, asserting that the victim-employee's involvement could lead to pressure for a less favorable plea offer or force the case to trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's order disqualifying the Maricopa County Attorney's Office and remanded the case for reconsideration, instructing the trial court to apply the Gomez factors and consider Durand's due process rights and the victim's rights.

title: Neptune Swimming Foundation v. City of Scottsdale
description: Whether the City of Scottsdale violated the Gift Clause by not considering a higher bid when awarding a license for aquatic center use, and whether the City abused its discretion by canceling a Request for Proposal (RFP) process.
plaintiff_argument: Neptune argued the City violated the Gift Clause by awarding a license at below-market rates and abused its discretion by canceling the RFP and not awarding Neptune the license as the most advantageous bidder.
defendant_argument: The City argued it did not violate the Gift Clause, as non-pecuniary benefits were considered, and did not abuse its discretion by canceling the RFP, asserting the procurement code served only as a guide.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed summary judgment for the City on the Gift Clause claim, finding no violation, but reversed summary judgment for the City on the procurement code claim, remanding for further proceedings to determine if the City abused its discretion.

title: Cao v. PFP Dorsey Investments
description: Whether the Arizona Condominium Act, specifically § 33-1228(C), authorized the forced sale of individual condominium units rather than the entire condominium property, and whether the statute as applied violated the eminent domain provision of the Arizona Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Xias argued that the forced sale of their unit violated § 33-1228(C) because it prohibited the forced sale of less than an entire condominium, and alternatively, that § 33-1228 was unconstitutional as it authorized a taking of private property for private use.
defendant_argument: PFP Dorsey Investments, LLC, and the Association argued that the sale complied with § 33-1228 and that the Xias contractually agreed to the terms of the Declaration, which incorporated the Condominium Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' decision, affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the eminent domain claim, but reversed on the interpretation of § 33-1228(C), holding that it authorized only the sale of all condominium property, not individual units, if a forced sale occurred. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

title: State v. Santillanes
description: Whether the State has the right to appeal a trial court's order granting expungement and restoration of civil rights, or whether it may seek relief only through a petition for special action.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued it has the right to appeal expungement orders under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4) because such orders affect its substantial rights.
defendant_argument: Santillanes argued that A.R.S. § 36-2862(F) provides the exclusive grounds for appeal in expungement cases, allowing only petitioners to appeal denials, and that an expungement order does not affect the State's substantial rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the State has the right to appeal an order expunging records pertaining to a felony conviction and restoring civil rights under A.R.S. § 13-4032(4), vacating parts of the court of appeals' opinion and remanding for further proceedings.

title: Planned Parenthood of Arizona v. Hazelrigg
description: Whether the Arizona Legislature's later abortion statutes in Title 36, particularly A.R.S. § 36-2322, repealed or restricted the earlier near-total abortion ban under A.R.S. § 13-3603.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that A.R.S. § 36-2322 implicitly authorizes abortions up to fifteen weeks' gestation, thereby repealing or restricting the older, near-total ban in A.R.S. § 13-3603.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General and intervenors argued that A.R.S. § 36-2322 does not create an independent right to abortion and that A.R.S. § 13-3603 remains enforceable after Roe v. Wade was overturned.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment vacating the injunction of A.R.S. § 13-3603, making the near-total abortion ban enforceable, and vacated the court of appeals' opinion and stay of enforcement.

title: Torres v. Jai Dining Services
description: Whether the anti-abrogation clause extends to dram-shop actions recognized after statehood, thereby preventing the legislature from limiting such actions.
plaintiff_argument: The anti-abrogation clause protects the common law dram-shop action, which evolved from pre-statehood negligence rights, and thus the legislature cannot limit it.
defendant_argument: The anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were created after statehood, allowing the legislature to limit them.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the anti-abrogation clause does not protect dram-shop actions because they were recognized after statehood, thus affirming the legislature's ability to limit such actions and ruling in favor of JAI Dining Services.

title: Draper v. Gentry
description: Whether a criminal defendant can compel a crime victim to produce their personal vehicle for GPS data extraction by the defendant's agent for in camera inspection, balancing the defendant's right to a complete defense against the victim's constitutional and statutory rights to privacy and to refuse discovery.
plaintiff_argument: Draper argued that compelling him to produce his truck for GPS data extraction violated his constitutional rights against unreasonable search and seizure and his victim's rights to refuse discovery and privacy, and that a higher standard (probable cause or substantial probability) should apply.
defendant_argument: Nez argued he needed the GPS data to present a complete third-party defense and for cross-examination, and that the less stringent "reasonable possibility" standard should apply for in camera review.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's order, remanding the case for the trial court to apply a clarified standard: the "reasonable possibility" standard if data extraction ensures only the court sees the data, but the more demanding "substantial probability" standard if the defendant's agent will view any portion of the data.

title: State v. Purcell
description: Whether the court of appeals had appellate jurisdiction over the dismissal of resentencing proceedings for juvenile offenders, with petitioners arguing for jurisdiction and the state arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the resentencing proceedings were not post-conviction relief (PCR) proceedings and that the trial court's orders affected their substantial rights, thus granting the court of appeals jurisdiction for a direct appeal.
defendant_argument: The state argued that the proceedings were PCR proceedings, and therefore, appellate review required a petition for review, not a direct appeal, meaning the court of appeals lacked jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Arizona concluded that the court of appeals had jurisdiction over the appeals in these cases and remanded them for further consideration.

title: State v. Brearcliffe
description: Whether a defendant's constitutional right to appeal can be divested under A.R.S. § 13-4033(C) without prior notice and an opportunity at sentencing to prove their absence was involuntary.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Johnson waived his right to appeal by absconding and that the statute does not require an express finding of involuntary absence by the trial court.
defendant_argument: Johnson argued that he was not afforded the opportunity to prove his absence was involuntary and that § 13-4033(C) is unconstitutional as a procedural law usurping the Court's rulemaking authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' order and remanded the case to the trial court to provide Johnson an opportunity to prove by clear and convincing evidence that his absence was involuntary.

title: Matthews v. The Industrial Commission of Arizona
description: Whether A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B), which limits workers' compensation claims for mental illnesses to those arising from "unexpected, unusual or extraordinary stress," violates Article 18, Section 8 of the Arizona Constitution or the equal protection guarantee of Article 2, Section 13.
plaintiff_argument: Matthews argued that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) is unconstitutional because it impermissibly restricts workers' compensation for mental injuries by requiring a higher standard of proof than for physical injuries, violating Article 18, Section 8 and equal protection.
defendant_argument: The City of Tucson and Tristar argued that the statute is constitutional, as the original Workers' Compensation Act did not contemplate mental injuries, and the incident Matthews experienced was not an "unexpected, unusual or extraordinary stress" situation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the ALJ's decision, ruling that A.R.S. § 23-1043.01(B) is constitutional and does not violate Article 18, Section 8 or the equal protection guarantee.

title: Burns v. Arizona Public Service Co.
description: Whether a majority of the Arizona Corporation Commission can prevent an individual commissioner from exercising their constitutional investigatory powers over public service corporations, and whether an aggrieved commissioner can seek judicial recourse.
plaintiff_argument: Robert Burns argued that individual commissioners have independent constitutional and statutory authority to inspect and investigate public service corporations and issue subpoenas, and that the Commission majority cannot quash these efforts.
defendant_argument: Arizona Public Service Company and the Commission argued that the Commission as a whole has plenary authority over rate-making proceedings and the power to establish rules, meaning individual commissioners' investigatory powers are subordinate to the majority's decisions within such proceedings.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that a majority of commissioners cannot prevent an individual commissioner from exercising their investigatory powers and that an aggrieved commissioner can seek judicial recourse.

title: Leibsohn v. Hobbs
description: Whether signatures collected by initiative petition circulators should be disqualified for failing to strictly comply with statutory registration requirements regarding residence address unit numbers and the submission of multiple affidavits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that signatures should be disqualified because circulators failed to strictly comply with statutory requirements by not listing unit numbers in multi-unit housing addresses and not submitting a new affidavit for each initiative petition.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that a unit number is not explicitly required in a residence address and that one affidavit should suffice for multiple initiatives, further asserting that the Secretary of State's registration procedures made strict compliance with the affidavit requirement impossible.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that a unit number is not required in a circulator's residence address and declining to disqualify signatures for noncompliance with the multiple affidavit requirement because the Secretary's procedures made compliance impossible, thereby protecting the constitutional right to the initiative process.

title: Arizona Free Enterprise Club v. Hobbs
description: Whether tax revenue measures, including those that may decrease net revenue, are exempt from the referendum process if they are for the support and maintenance of existing state departments and institutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Arizona Free Enterprise Club, argued that Senate Bill 1828 (SB 1828) is a tax revenue measure for the support and maintenance of state departments and institutions, and is therefore exempt from the referendum process, regardless of whether it increases or decreases revenue.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Invest in Arizona, contended that SB 1828 was subject to referendum because it did not qualify as a 'support and maintenance' measure, and that only appropriation measures, or tax measures that increase revenue, are exempt from referendum.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Arizona reversed the trial court's ruling, holding that SB 1828, as a revenue measure for the support and maintenance of existing state departments and institutions, is exempt from the referendum process, irrespective of its effect on revenue.

title: Fann v. Kemp
description: Whether legislative privilege protects communications related to an election audit from public disclosure, with the plaintiff arguing against such protection and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: American Oversight argued that the audit communications are public records subject to disclosure, not protected by legislative privilege, especially if administrative or political, or if the privilege was waived.
defendant_argument: The Arizona Senate argued that the audit communications are protected by legislative privilege because the audit was a legitimate legislative activity within the legislature's authority to investigate and propose legislation, and the privilege was not waived.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's order to disclose all communications concerning the Audit, vacated the court of appeals' opinion, and remanded the case for the trial court to resolve the Senate's legislative privilege claims consistent with the Supreme Court's broader interpretation of legislative privilege.

title: Willis v. Bernini
description: Whether the Arizona Constitution guarantees a due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of clearly exculpatory evidence to a grand jury, and what standard defines "clearly exculpatory evidence" that a prosecutor must present, especially concerning justification defenses.
plaintiff_argument: Willis argued that the State withheld clearly exculpatory evidence related to a justification defense, which prosecutors are obligated to present to a grand jury, and that "clearly exculpatory evidence" should be defined as evidence that "might deter" a grand jury from finding probable cause.
defendant_argument: The State contended it fulfilled its obligations, did not withhold clearly exculpatory evidence, and asserted that there is no constitutional due process right to a fair and impartial presentation of evidence before a grand jury. It also argued for a narrower definition of "clearly exculpatory evidence" (Hogan's standard) or that the existing "would deter" standard was sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's denial of Willis's 12.9 Motion and remanded the case for a redetermination of probable cause, ruling that the State failed to present clearly exculpatory evidence, thereby denying Willis a substantial procedural right.

title: State v. Robinson
description: Whether the trial court erred in affirming Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson's convictions and death sentences, with Robinson arguing for reversal based on alleged errors in jury selection, aggravating circumstances, and life imprisonment instructions, and the State of Arizona arguing for affirmation.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Arizona argued that the trial court correctly denied Robinson's Batson challenges, properly found aggravating circumstances, and provided a legally sound life imprisonment instruction, thus his convictions and sentences should be affirmed.
defendant_argument: Robinson argued that the trial court erred in denying his Batson challenges, that the jury's findings of aggravating circumstances were flawed, and that the life imprisonment instruction was legally defective, warranting a reversal of his convictions and sentences.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Dwandarrius Jamar Robinson's convictions and sentences for two counts of first-degree murder, one count of arson, and one count of kidnapping.

title: State v. Reed
description: Whether a victim's attorney fees are recoverable as criminal restitution and, if so, to what extent, with the plaintiff arguing they are recoverable as a direct result of the criminal conduct, and the defendant arguing they are consequential damages not directly caused by the criminal conduct.
plaintiff_argument: The court properly ordered the fees because the victim's involvement in a contentious trial and necessity to retain counsel was a direct result of the defendant's criminal conduct.
defendant_argument: The trial court improperly ordered payment of the victim's attorney fees as restitution because those fees did not flow directly from the criminal conduct but instead constituted consequential damages.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's restitution order to the extent it ordered payment of the victim's attorney fees, except for two specific billing entries, and remanded the case to determine if those specific amounts should be ordered as restitution.

title: Arizona School Boards Association,  Inc. v. State
description: Whether four legislative budget reconciliation bills (HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819) violate the Arizona Constitution's "title requirement" or "single subject rule," with the plaintiffs arguing they do and the defendant arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs alleged that all four budget reconciliation bills violated the constitutional title requirement and that SB 1819 also violated the single subject rule, requesting they be declared unconstitutional and unenforceable.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the bills' titles satisfied the constitutional title requirement as they related to the general subject matter, and that the court lacked authority to rule on these issues, presenting a non-justiciable political question.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that the challenged sections of HB 2898, SB 1824, SB 1825, and SB 1819 violated the title requirement and that SB 1819 entirely violated the single subject rule, rendering them unconstitutional and void.

title: Fay v. Fox
description: Whether a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order, with the plaintiff arguing for this right and the defendant arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Beth Fay, argued that she has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the defendant's motion for a delayed appeal of a restitution order because it implicates her rights to due process, prompt restitution, and finality, and could delay or extinguish her restitution award.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Jordan Michael Hanson, argued that victims do not have a general right to be heard in post-conviction relief proceedings, or specifically on claims for permission to take a delayed appeal from a Criminal Restitution Order, unless such a right is expressly provided by law.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals decision and reversed the trial court judgment, holding that a crime victim has a constitutional and statutory right to be heard on the merits of a Rule 32.1(f) motion for a delayed appeal to contest a restitution award.

title: Fann v. State
description: Whether Proposition 208, a voter initiative imposing an income tax surcharge for school funding, violates the Education Expenditure Clause by exceeding expenditure limits and the Tax Enactment Clause by imposing a new tax without a supermajority vote.
plaintiff_argument: Fann argues Prop. 208's direct funding to schools violates the Education Expenditure Clause because the funds are local revenues subject to expenditure limits, not exempt grants, and that Prop. 208 also violates the Tax Enactment Clause by imposing a new tax without a supermajority legislative vote.
defendant_argument: Invest in Education argues Prop. 208 funds are "grants" exempt from the Education Expenditure Clause's expenditure limits, and that the Tax Enactment Clause, requiring a supermajority vote for new taxes, does not apply to voter initiatives.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of a preliminary injunction, ruling that Proposition 208's direct funding is unconstitutional to the extent it exceeds the Education Expenditure Clause's expenditure limits and its non-revenue provisions are not severable, but also ruled that the Tax Enactment Clause does not apply to voter initiatives, and remanded the case to determine the actual expenditure limit violation.

title: Redgrave v. Ducey
description: Whether Arizona has consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the minimum wage or overtime provisions of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Arizona has waived its sovereign immunity to FLSA claims, either by removing the case to federal court or as a matter of law, and that the rule favoring government liability extends to federal damages claims.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Arizona legislature has not unequivocally consented to federal damages liability, and therefore, the state retains its sovereign immunity under the FLSA.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arizona has not consented to damages liability for a state agency's violation of the FLSA's minimum wage or overtime provisions because the legislature has not expressly or unequivocally implied such consent.

title: State v. Bigger
description: Whether a defendant must present an expert affidavit to support an ineffective assistance of counsel claim, whether Perry v. New Hampshire caused a significant change in Arizona law, and whether A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with Arizona Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.4 regarding post-conviction relief filing deadlines.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Ronald Bigger, argued that he received ineffective assistance of counsel, that Perry v. New Hampshire constituted a significant change in law entitling him to relief, and that A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) unconstitutionally conflicts with court rules regarding untimely post-conviction relief filings.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Arizona, argued that Bigger had not proven his ineffective assistance of counsel claims, that Perry v. New Hampshire did not cause a significant change in Arizona law, and that the statute regarding post-conviction relief filing deadlines was constitutional or supplemental to court rules.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the court of appeals' opinion and affirmed the trial court's ruling dismissing Bigger's post-conviction relief petition, while also clarifying that an expert affidavit is not required for ineffective assistance of counsel claims, Perry v. New Hampshire did not change Arizona law, and A.R.S. § 13-4234(G) is unconstitutional as applied.

title: Mesnard v. Campagnolo
description: Whether a legislator is absolutely immune from liability for defamation when modifying an investigatory report and issuing a news release, under the legislative immunity doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: Mesnard argued he was absolutely immune from defamation liability for both the investigatory report and the news release because these actions constituted legislative functions.
defendant_argument: Shooter argued Mesnard was not immune because his actions, particularly the modifications to the report and the news release, were not legitimate legislative functions and denied due process.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of Mesnard's motion to dismiss regarding the news release, but reversed the denial of dismissal regarding the investigatory report, remanding for further proceedings on the news release claims.

title: State v. Patel
description: Whether A.R.S. § 28-672(G), which limits the amount of restitution that can be awarded to a victim for loss resulting from a violation of specified traffic offenses, is either an unconstitutional limitation on the right to receive restitution or a valid legislative enactment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the Victims' Bill of Rights (VBR) guarantees a right to full restitution, and the statutory limitation was unconstitutional as it conflicted with this constitutional right.
defendant_argument: Patel argued that the VBR's plain language does not require "full" restitution, and the legislature has the authority to limit restitution amounts.
decision_outcome: The court held that the constitutional right to receive restitution guaranteed by the VBR is a right to receive the full amount of economic loss or injury caused by a defendant's criminal conduct, and therefore, § 28-672(G)'s limitation on a restitution award is unconstitutional and void, reinstating the municipal court's restitution order of $61,191.99.

title: State ex rel. Brnovich v. City of Tucson
description: Whether Arizona Revised Statutes § 16-204.01, which mandates consolidating local elections with state and national elections when voter turnout decreases, can apply to a charter city whose charter requires electing local officials on non-statewide election dates.
plaintiff_argument: The state law § 16-204.01 should apply to the City of Tucson because increasing voter turnout in local elections is a matter of statewide concern, and low turnout adversely affects the fundamental right to vote and electoral integrity.
defendant_argument: The City of Tucson's charter provision requiring off-cycle elections is a matter of purely municipal concern, and the state law cannot preempt its local autonomy in structuring its government.
decision_outcome: The court held that Arizona Revised Statutes § 16-204.01 is unconstitutional as applied to the City of Tucson's charter, allowing the city to continue holding off-cycle municipal elections.

title: Schires v. Carlat
description: Whether the City of Peoria violated the Arizona Constitution's Gift Clause by using public funds to incentivize a private university to open a branch campus.
plaintiff_argument: The City's payments to Huntington University and Arrowhead Equities violated the Gift Clause because the value received by the public was far exceeded by the public funds paid, constituting an impermissible subsidy to private entities.
defendant_argument: The City's payments served a public purpose by stimulating economic development and revitalizing an underused area, and the economic benefits constituted sufficient consideration under the Gift Clause.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's judgment, ruling in favor of the Taxpayers and finding that the City violated the Gift Clause.

title: State v. Mixton
description: Whether the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution or article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires law enforcement officials to secure a judicially-authorized search warrant or order to obtain a user's Internet Protocol (IP) address or subscriber information voluntarily provided to an Internet Service Provider (ISP), with the State arguing no warrant is required and Mixton arguing such information is protected.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that neither the federal nor the Arizona Constitution requires a search warrant or court order to obtain IP addresses and ISP subscriber information.
defendant_argument: Mixton argues that both the Fourth Amendment and the Arizona Constitution protect IP addresses and ISP subscriber information, requiring a search warrant or court order.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Mixton's convictions, holding that neither the Fourth Amendment nor article 2, section 8 of the Arizona Constitution requires a search warrant or court order for law enforcement to obtain IP addresses or ISP subscriber information, as this information is not considered a 'private affair' under the third-party doctrine.
